docs.title: NexusAI Data Platform
docs.text: Welcome to the comprehensive documentation portal for the NexusAI Data Platform -- an enterprise-grade AI operating layer that connects your systems, builds semantic context, and deploys autonomous agents that reason and act across your organization.

docs.title: What is NexusAI?
docs.text: NexusAI is the Intelligent AI Operating Layer for the Enterprise. Rather than replacing existing systems, NexusAI sits on top of your current technology stack -- CRMs, ERPs, data warehouses, and operational tools -- and unifies them into a single, AI-driven intelligence fabric. It transforms siloed enterprise data into connected, actionable knowledge that autonomous agents use to reason, decide, and execute.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
NexusAI operates through a four-stage pipeline that turns disconnected enterprise data into autonomous action:

Stage Description Connect Plug into existing enterprise systems -- CRM, ERP, data warehouses, SaaS tools -- via pre-built connectors and APIs. No data migration or system replacement required. Map Build a semantic knowledge graph that captures entities, relationships, and business context across all connected systems. Reason The AI Reasoning Engine applies structured reasoning (ReAct) across the connected knowledge graph to analyze situations, identify patterns, and determine optimal actions. Execute Autonomous agents carry out end-to-end workflows -- updating records, triggering processes, escalating exceptions -- with full auditability and human-in-the-loop controls.

docs.title: Key Capabilities
docs.text:
Enterprise Data Integration

Pre-built connectors for CRM, ERP, data warehouses, and SaaS platforms. Unified data access layer with real-time and batch ingestion. Zero-migration architecture -- NexusAI connects to systems in place.

Semantic Intelligence Layer

Automated knowledge graph construction from connected data sources. Entity resolution, relationship mapping, and contextual enrichment. A living semantic model that evolves as your data changes.

AI Reasoning Engine (ReAct)

Structured Reasoning + Acting framework for multi-step decision-making. Cross-system analysis that no single tool can perform alone. Transparent reasoning traces for auditability and compliance.

Autonomous Execution

AI agents that carry out complex, multi-step workflows end to end. Human-in-the-loop guardrails for high-stakes decisions. Full audit trail of every action taken and every decision made.

docs.title: NexusAI Backend (Call Processing Engine)
docs.text:
Technology Stack: - Framework: Python 3.11+, FastAPI - Protocol: Model Context Protocol (MCP) with HTTP Gateway - AWS SDK: boto3 for AWS service integration - AI: OpenAI GPT for transcription and analysis

MCP Tools: | Tool | Description | |------|-------------| | journeys_tool | Journey, stage, and job management | | logs_and_reports_tool | Logs and report generation | | wxcc_simulator_tool | WXCC simulator operations | | license_tool | License activation and validation |

REST APIs: | Endpoint | Description | |----------|-------------| | /api/v1/journeys/* | Journey management | | /api/v1/license/* | License management | | /api/v1/simulator/* | WXCC Simulator APIs | | /api/v1/analytics/* | Analytics and metrics | | /api/v1/calls/* | Processed calls data | | /health | Health check |

Call Processing Stages: 1. Fetch Tasks - Retrieve tasks from Webex CC 2. Deduplication - Check for already-processed tasks 3. Process Recordings - Download, transcribe, upload 4. Register Metadata - Create metadata and Glue partitions 5. AI Analysis - GPT-powered call analysis

docs.title: NexusAI KPI Definitions
docs.text: Project: NexusAI Enterprise Analytics Document Version: 1.0 Date: March 11, 2026

docs.title: 1.1 Quick Stats
docs.text: KPI Business Definition Formula / Logic Implementation Constants / Thresholds Overall QA Score Weighted quality assurance score across all analyzed calls avg(grading.total_score_percent) across all calls in the filtered set Backend: qa_aggregation_service.py — averages total_score_percent from all call grading results. Frontend: qaAnalyticsService.ts getSummaryStats() — reads analysis_summary.overall_team_score, rounds to integer — Compliance Rate Percentage of calls that pass PDPA compliance (calls where pdpa_pass = true / total_calls) × 100 Frontend: qaAnalyticsService.ts calculateComplianceRate() — filters individual_call_analysis for compliance.pdpa_pass === true, divides by total, rounds to 1 decimal Pass = pdpa_pass === true Total Revenue Impact Aggregate estimated deal value across the pipeline sum(deal_potential.estimated_value) over all filtered calls Frontend: MainQADashboard.tsx — reduces filteredCalls summing deal_potential.estimated_value. Backend: qa_aggregation_service.py total_pipeline_value — Qualifying Questions Rate Success rate of qualifying questions asked by reps Per call: asked.length / (asked.length + missed.length) × 100. Then: avg across all calls Frontend: qaAnalyticsService.ts calculateQualifyingQuestionsRate() — per-call ratio averaged, rounded to 1 decimal. Legacy fallback: compliance_rate field —

docs.title: 1.2 Revenue KPI Cards
docs.text: KPI Business Definition Formula / Logic Implementation Constants / Thresholds High Probability Deals Total value of deals with high win probability sum(estimated_value) for calls where probability > 0.7 Frontend: MainQADashboard.tsx — reduces filteredCalls, accumulates estimated_value only when deal_potential.probability > 0.7. Backend: qa_aggregation_service.py uses same threshold Threshold: probability > 0.7 (70%) Monthly Revenue Projection Projected monthly revenue from the pipeline totalPipelineValue × 0.33 Frontend: MainQADashboard.tsx — multiplies total pipeline by 0.33 (assumes 1/3 of pipeline converts monthly). Backend: sum(estimated_value × probability) per call (probability-weighted) Factor: 0.33 (frontend), probability-weighted (backend) Coaching ROI Potential (aka Revenue Increase Potential) Potential revenue uplift from coaching interventions on underperforming calls with low-probability deals sum(deal_value × (1 − probability)) for calls where total_score_percent < 70 AND probability < 0.7 Frontend: MainQADashboard.tsx — filters calls by QA score < 70% and probability < 70%, sums deal_value × (1 − probability). Backend: qa_aggregation_service.py uses same logic Thresholds: QA score < 70%, probability < 0.7 (70%) Deals at Risk Count of deals with a composite risk score above the at-risk threshold Count of deals where riskScore > 0.75. The risk score combines close probability (40%), call quality (25%), risk factor count (up to 20%), and customer sentiment (15%) into a single 0–1 value Frontend: MainQADashboard.tsx — computes riskScore per deal via calculateRiskScore(), counts deals exceeding 0.75. Backend: qa_aggregation_service.py uses same logic Threshold: riskScore > 0.75

docs.title: 1.3 Charts and Sections
docs.text: KPI Business Definition Formula / Logic Implementation Constants / Thresholds Performance by QA Category Average scores across 6 QA categories, derived from 16 grading elements Each category = average of mapped element scores across all calls. Categories and element mappings: (1) Call Opening & Closing = avg(Greetings & Intro, Call Closing); (2) Verification = avg(Verification & Validation); (3) Product Knowledge & Selling = avg(Needs Assessment, Product/Service Presentation, Objection Handling, Sales Tenacity, Closing Technique, Upsell & Cross-sell); (4) Communication Skills = avg(Clarity of Verbal Expression, Active Listening, Telephony Skill & Etiquette); (5) Include NPS = avg(NPS Prompt); (6) Operational System Proficiency = avg(Activity Log, Opportunity Handling, Respond to Customer Queries) Frontend: qaAnalyticsService.ts calculateQACategories() — maps each grading element name (case-insensitive includes) to a category, sums scores, divides by (element count × total calls) Element name matching is case-insensitive substring Rep Score Distribution Agent performance spread with individual rankings Per call: for each grading element with weight > 0 and not in N/A list, apply score >= 75 ? 100 : 0, then sum(passFailScore × weight) / totalWeight. Per agent: avg(call scores). Agents sorted by score descending and ranked Frontend: qaAnalyticsService.ts getAllAgentsForDistribution() Pass threshold: >= 75. N/A elements: NPS Prompt, Activity Log, Opportunity Handling, Respond to Customer Queries Top Performers Leading agents by overall QA score Agents ranked by average weighted pass/fail score (same formula as Rep Score Distribution), top 3 displayed with call count and score Frontend: qaAnalyticsService.ts getTopPerformers(data, 3) — uses backend top_performers order if available, recalculates scores, filters agents with calls > 0 Limit: 3 Top Deals Highest value opportunities Calls filtered to estimated_value > 0, sorted by deal_potential.estimated_value descending, top 3 shown Frontend: MainQADashboard.tsx — filter, sort, slice(0, 3) Limit: 3 Recent Alerts Quality issues requiring attention with priority indicators Alerts generated from call analysis: High priority for PDPA compliance breach (pdpa_pass = false) or low call score (total_score_percent < 50). Alerts filtered by current rep/date selection. Display capped at 10 Backend: qa_aggregation_service.py _aggregate() — generates alerts. Frontend: qaAnalyticsService.ts getRecentAlerts() — filters by active call IDs/agents, maps priority to display High: PDPA breach or score < 50. Display limit: 10

docs.title: 2.1 Call Overview Cards
docs.text: KPI Business Definition Formula / Logic Implementation Constants / Thresholds Total Calls Count of analyzed calls in the current filter count(individual_call_analysis) after rep, date, and search filters Frontend: CallAnalysisDashboard.tsx — searchedCalls.length — Team Score Average QA score across filtered calls avg(grading.total_score_percent) over filtered calls, rounded to integer Frontend: CallAnalysisDashboard.tsx — reduces searchedCalls using getOverallScore(call) which returns call.grading.total_score_percent — Average Duration Mean call duration Parse each call's call_duration ("M:SS"), convert to seconds, average, reformat to "M:SS" Backend: qa_aggregation_service.py _compute_average_duration() — Compliance Rate Percentage of PDPA-compliant calls Same formula as Executive Summary: (pdpa_pass true count / total) × 100 Frontend: qaAnalyticsService.ts calculateComplianceRate() Pass = pdpa_pass === true Revenue at Risk Total deal value of all deals classified as at-risk sum(deal_value) for all deals where riskScore > 0.75 (i.e., the monetary value of the "Deals at Risk" set) Backend: qa_aggregation_service.py — sums deal values for deals exceeding the risk score threshold. Frontend: CallAnalysisDashboard.tsx computes riskScore per deal and sums values Threshold: riskScore > 0.75

docs.title: 2.2 Individual Call QA Score
docs.text: KPI Business Definition Formula / Logic Implementation Constants / Thresholds Overall QA Score Per-call quality score grading.total_score_percent (0-100) as computed by AI analysis Frontend: CallAnalysisDashboard.tsx getOverallScore() — returns call.grading.total_score_percent — QA Pass/Fail (Table) Visual badge in call list total_score_percent >= 90 = Pass (green), < 90 = Fail (red) Frontend: CallAnalysisDashboard.tsx — badge color logic Pass: >= 90 QA Pass/Fail (Report) Pass/fail in PDF report total_score_percent >= 75 = Pass, < 75 = Fail Frontend: CallAnalysisDashboard.tsx report section Pass: >= 75

docs.title: 2.3 Compliance and Sentiment
docs.text: KPI Business Definition Formula / Logic Implementation Constants / Thresholds PDPA Compliance Per-call compliance status Binary: compliance.pdpa_pass === true → 100 (Pass), false → 0 (Fail). Includes breach list and professional conduct assessment Frontend: CallAnalysisDashboard.tsx getComplianceScore(). Backend AI: ai_analyzer.py — prompt checks for PDPA breaches Pass = pdpa_pass === true Customer Sentiment Overall customer sentiment for a call sentiment_analysis.overall_sentiment × 100 (displayed as 0-100%) Frontend: CallAnalysisDashboard.tsx — Math.round(call.sentiment_analysis.overall_sentiment * 100). Backend: ai_analyzer.py — keyword-based fallback: (positive_count - negative_count) / (positive_count + negative_count), normalized from [-1,1] to [0,1] via (sentiment + 1) / 2 Range: 0-100% Sentiment Progression Sentiment change over the course of a call Transcript split into 5 equal chunks; average sentiment per chunk produces a 5-point progression array Backend: ai_analyzer.py — divides segment_sentiments into 5 chunks, averages each. Frontend: transcriptService.ts — linear interpolation to match transcript segment count Max 5 data points Key Sentiment Moments Points in the call where sentiment shifted significantly Segments where abs(current_sentiment - previous_sentiment) > 0.2 Frontend: transcriptService.ts — flags segments exceeding the threshold Change threshold: > 0.2

docs.title: 2.4 QA Scoring Breakdown
docs.text:
The AI scores each call against 16 grading elements. Each element receives a score (0-100) with evidence quotes.

Element Weight Category Greetings & Intro 5 Call Opening & Closing Call Closing 5 Call Opening & Closing Verification & Validation 5 Verification Needs Assessment 10 Product Knowledge & Selling Product/Service Presentation 10 Product Knowledge & Selling Objection Handling 10 Product Knowledge & Selling Sales Tenacity & Determination 10 Product Knowledge & Selling Closing Technique & Follow-Up 10 Product Knowledge & Selling Upsell & Cross-sell 10 Product Knowledge & Selling Clarity of Verbal Expression 5 Communication Skills Active Listening 5 Communication Skills Telephony Skill & Etiquette 10 Communication Skills NPS Prompt 10 Include NPS Activity Log 15 Operational System Proficiency Opportunity Handling 15 Operational System Proficiency Respond to Customer Queries 15 Operational System Proficiency

Total weight: 150

Per-element pass/fail logic (frontend weighted scoring):

  • If element score >= 75 → passFailScore = 100
  • If element score < 75 → passFailScore = 0
  • Weighted score = sum(passFailScore × weight) / sum(weight) (excluding N/A elements)

AI prompt pass threshold: 70% (backend ai_analyzer.py)

N/A elements (excluded from weighted scoring in Rep Score Distribution): NPS Prompt, Activity Log, Opportunity Handling, Respond to Customer Queries

docs.title: 4.2 Risk Assessment
docs.text:
KPI Business Definition Formula / Logic Implementation Constants / Thresholds Risk Score Composite risk indicator for a deal, combining four weighted signals into a single 0–1 value. A deal is "at risk" when this score exceeds 0.75 (1 - probability) × 0.4 + (1 - overallScore/100) × 0.25 + min(riskFactorCount × 0.05, 0.2) + (1 - sentimentScore) × 0.15, capped at 1.0 Frontend: DealAnalysisDashboard.tsx calculateRiskScore() Weights: Probability 40%, Performance 25%, Risk Factors 5%/factor (max 20%), Sentiment 15%. Cap: 1.0. At-risk threshold: > 0.75 Risk Level Categorical risk classification based on the composite risk score Low: riskScore <= 0.4. Medium: riskScore > 0.4 AND <= 0.75. High: riskScore > 0.75 Frontend: DealAnalysisDashboard.tsx — risk distribution calculation Low: <= 0.4, Medium: 0.4–0.75, High: > 0.75

How the Risk Score works (plain language):

The risk score is a single number between 0 and 1. It adds four pieces together, each making the score higher when things look worse:

  1. Close chance (40% of the score): The lower the probability the deal will close, the more risk. "Unlikely to close" pushes the score up.
  2. Call quality (25% of the score): The lower the QA score for the call, the more risk. "Poor call" pushes the score up.
  3. Number of risk factors (up to 20% of the score): Each risk factor (e.g., contract issues, competitor mentions) adds a bit. The more factors the higher this part, but it stops increasing after a point (capped at 20%).
  4. Customer sentiment (15% of the score): The more negative the customer sounded on the call, the more risk. "Unhappy customer" pushes the score up.

The four parts are added together and the result is capped at 1.0. A deal is classified as "at risk" when this number exceeds 0.75.

docs.title: Where Calculations Happen
docs.text:
The NexusAI architecture splits KPI computation between the backend aggregation service and the frontend dashboard components. Understanding which layer computes what is critical for debugging discrepancies.

Backend (qa_aggregation_service.py):

  • overall_team_score — avg(grading.total_score_percent)
  • compliance_rate — (pdpa_pass true count / total) × 100
  • average_call_duration — parsed and averaged from call metadata
  • revenue_impact.total_pipeline_value — sum(deal_potential.estimated_value)
  • revenue_impact.high_probability_deals — sum(estimated_value) where probability > 0.7
  • revenue_impact.at_risk_deals — count where riskScore > 0.75
  • revenue_impact.revenue_at_risk — sum(deal_value) where riskScore > 0.75
  • revenue_impact.coaching_roi_potential — sum(deal_value × (1 − probability)) where QA score < 70% and probability < 0.7
  • revenue_impact.monthly_revenue_projection — sum(estimated_value × probability) (probability-weighted)
  • areas_for_improvement — bottom 5 elements by avg score
  • coaching_opportunities — agents with avg score < 75
  • alerts_and_flags — PDPA breaches and low scores

Frontend overrides (when rep/date filters are applied):

  • total_pipeline_value → sum(deal_potential.estimated_value) over filtered calls
  • high_probability_deals → sum(estimated_value) where probability > 0.7 over filtered calls
  • coaching_roi_potential → sum(deal_value × (1 − probability)) for calls where QA score < 70% and probability < 0.7
  • monthly_revenue_projection → totalPipeline × 0.33 (simplified from backend's probability-weighted formula)
  • at_risk_deals → count of deals where riskScore > 0.75, re-computed from filtered deal set
  • revenue_at_risk → sum(deal_value) where riskScore > 0.75

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
This document defines the User Acceptance Testing (UAT) test cases for the NexusAI platform delivered under the NexusAI Platform SOW. Test cases are organized by SOW feature category and map directly to the deliverables defined in SOW Section 4 ("In Scope Capabilities") and the detailed dashboard functionality tables (SOW pages 9-14).

Descoped Items:

  • B-2 Lead Conversion — Descoped per CR-001. NexusAI creates Leads only; Lead-to-Opportunity conversion remains a manual action by NexusAI Sales team.

Out of Scope (Future Phases):

  • Product Recommendations Engine (SOW Section 5)
  • Automatic Quote Generation (SOW Section 5)
  • Office 365 Integration & Email Analysis (SOW Section 5)
  • WhatsApp Integration (SOW Section 5)

docs.title: Data Sources
docs.text:
In the context of ontology-driven data architecture (e.g., enterprise knowledge graph, semantic layer, or ontology-backed analytics), FDW, ETL, and CDC represent three different integration patterns for bringing source data into alignment with your ontology.

Below is a clear side-by-side comparison, followed by when to use each.

docs.title: 🔹 What It Is
docs.text:
FDW is a virtualization approach. The ontology layer queries external data sources live without physically moving the data.

Example:

  • Postgres FDW
  • Trino/Presto connectors
  • Data virtualization tools

docs.title: 🔹 How It Works in Ontology
docs.text:
• Ontology defines semantic model.
  • Tables in external systems are mapped to ontology entities.
  • Queries are pushed down to source systems.
  • No data replication.

docs.title: 🔹 Architecture Pattern
docs.text: Source DB → (FDW) → Semantic/Ontology Layer → User

docs.title: 🔹 Pros
docs.text: ✔ No data duplication ✔ Real-time access ✔ Faster to implement ✔ Lower storage cost ✔ Good for exploratory or federated setups

docs.title: 🔹 Cons
docs.text: ✖ Query performance depends on source system ✖ Complex joins across systems can be slow ✖ Harder to optimize analytics ✖ Source system availability impacts ontology

docs.title: 🔹 Best Use Cases
docs.text:
• Real-time dashboards
  • Low-latency operational analytics
  • Small-to-medium datasets
  • When governance restricts copying data

docs.title: 🔹 What It Is
docs.text: Data is copied, transformed, and loaded into a central store (data warehouse/lake) aligned with ontology schema.

docs.title: 🔹 How It Works in Ontology
docs.text:
• Extract from source
  • Transform to ontology model (entities/relationships)
  • Load into semantic DB or warehouse

docs.title: 🔹 Architecture Pattern
docs.text: Source → ETL → Ontology-Aligned Warehouse → Semantic Layer → User

docs.title: 🔹 Pros
docs.text: ✔ High performance queries ✔ Data consistency ✔ Historical snapshots possible ✔ Better for analytics and ML ✔ Full control over schema

docs.title: 🔹 Cons
docs.text: ✖ Data duplication ✖ Latency (batch-based unless near-real-time ETL) ✖ More infrastructure ✖ Higher cost

docs.title: 🔹 Best Use Cases
docs.text:
• Enterprise knowledge graphs
  • ML feature engineering
  • Complex cross-domain analytics
  • Regulatory reporting
  • Historical analysis

docs.title: 🔹 What It Is
docs.text:
CDC captures incremental changes from source systems and streams them into ontology-aligned storage.

Often built using:

  • Debezium
  • Kafka
  • Database log-based replication

docs.title: 🔹 How It Works in Ontology
docs.text:
• Source DB changes detected from logs
  • Changes streamed
  • Ontology entities updated in near real-time

docs.title: 🔹 Architecture Pattern
docs.text: Source DB → CDC Stream → Transformation → Ontology Store

docs.title: 🔹 Pros
docs.text: ✔ Near real-time sync ✔ Efficient (incremental updates) ✔ Supports event-driven architecture ✔ Good for operational knowledge graphs

docs.title: 🔹 Cons
docs.text: ✖ More complex architecture ✖ Requires event streaming infra ✖ Harder debugging ✖ Schema evolution challenges

docs.title: 🔹 Best Use Cases
docs.text:
• Real-time enterprise graph
  • CRM updates reflected immediately
  • Fraud detection
  • Operational AI systems

docs.title: 🔎 Side-by-Side Comparison
docs.text: Feature FDW ETL CDC Data Copy ❌ No ✅ Yes ✅ Yes (incremental) Latency Real-time Batch Near real-time Performance Source dependent High High Historical Tracking Limited Excellent Good Infra Complexity Low Medium High Cost Low Medium-High Medium-High Best For Virtualization Analytics Streaming / Operational sync

docs.title: If your ontology is:
docs.text:
• A semantic query layer only → FDW may be enough.
  • A materialized knowledge graph → ETL or CDC is better.
  • A real-time enterprise graph → CDC is ideal.
  • A BI reporting layer → ETL is safest.

docs.title: 🎯 Decision Framework
docs.text:
Ask these questions:

  1. Do you need real-time updates?

  2. Yes → CDC or FDW

  3. No → ETL

  4. Do you need heavy cross-domain joins?

  5. Yes → ETL

  6. Is performance critical?

  7. Yes → ETL or CDC

  8. Do you want minimal infrastructure?

  9. Yes → FDW

  10. Is the ontology powering AI/ML?

  11. Yes → ETL or CDC

docs.title: 🏗 Hybrid Architecture (Very Common)
docs.text:
Most mature enterprises use:

  • CDC → core operational entities
  • ETL → historical + analytical layer
  • FDW → rare or low-value datasets

Hybrid example:

CRM → CDC → Enterprise Graph
Finance → ETL → Warehouse
Small tools → FDW

docs.title: 🚀 Executive Summary
docs.text:
• FDW = Virtual, Simple, Real-time, Lower Power
  • ETL = Stable, High-performance, Analytical Backbone
  • CDC = Real-time Enterprise-Grade Synchronization

how can i club this with CDC framework to frame a good ontogoy for finance domain

Great — this architecture is already ontology-first with R2RML/RML + RDF + TMF APIs + reasoner.

Now you want to club this with CDC to design a strong finance domain ontology framework.

Let’s do this systematically.

docs.title: 1️⃣ What Your Current Diagram Represents
docs.text:
Your current stack:

Source Systems (BSS / ERP / Files)
        ↓
R2RML / RDF ETL
        ↓
Semantic Integration Layer (Ontology + RDF)
        ↓
TMF APIs + Reasoner
        ↓
AI / Analytics

Right now it supports:

  • ETL-based transformation
  • Virtual mapping
  • RDF materialization
  • Ontology reasoning

But it is not real-time.

docs.title: 2️⃣ How CDC Fits Into This Architecture
docs.text:
Instead of batch ETL, we introduce log-based streaming updates from finance systems.

New pattern:

Finance DB (ERP / GL / AR / AP)
        ↓
Database Logs
        ↓
CDC Engine (Debezium / Kafka Connect)
        ↓
Streaming Transformer (RML Mapper / Stream Processor)
        ↓
RDF Triples (Incremental)
        ↓
Ontology Store (Graph DB)
        ↓
Reasoner + TMF APIs

So instead of:

"Extract everything and transform nightly"

We move to:

"Capture every financial event as it happens and update ontology incrementally"

docs.title: 3️⃣ Finance Domain: What Should Be Event-Driven?
docs.text:
In finance, most entities are event-based:

Finance Concept CDC Trigger Invoice Insert / Status change Payment Insert Journal Entry Insert GL Posting Insert Credit Note Insert FX Rate Update Update Budget Revision Update Expense Claim Status change

Finance is PERFECT for CDC because:

  • It’s transaction-heavy
  • Requires auditability
  • Needs near-real-time compliance monitoring
  • Supports fraud detection / risk scoring

docs.title: 4️⃣ Recommended Hybrid Architecture (For Finance Ontology)
docs.text:
You should NOT replace ETL completely.

Instead:

docs.title: ✅ Use CDC for:
docs.text:
• Transactions
  • Payments
  • AR/AP
  • Ledger entries
  • Approval workflows

docs.title: ✅ Use ETL for:
docs.text:
• Historical migration
  • Master data cleanup
  • Periodic reporting aggregates
  • Large static reference data

docs.title: ✅ Optional FDW for:
docs.text: • Rarely accessed legacy systems

docs.text:

docs.title: 6️⃣ Designing a Good Finance Ontology (Critical Part)
docs.text: Now the important part.

docs.title: A. Core Finance Ontology Modules
docs.text: Design ontology modularly:

docs.title: 1️⃣ Financial Entity Layer
docs.text:
• Account
  • Cost Center
  • Ledger
  • Journal Entry
  • Invoice
  • Payment
  • Vendor
  • Customer
  • Contract
  • Tax Code

docs.title: 2️⃣ Financial Event Layer
docs.text:
Model events explicitly:

  • InvoiceIssuedEvent
  • PaymentReceivedEvent
  • JournalPostedEvent
  • ApprovalGrantedEvent
  • BudgetExceededEvent

CDC events map directly here.

docs.title: B. Event-Driven Ontology Pattern
docs.text:
Instead of only modeling static entities:

Bad model:

Invoice → hasStatus → Paid

Better CDC-aware model:

Invoice123
    rdf:type Invoice
    hasEvent PaymentEvent456

PaymentEvent456
    rdf:type PaymentReceivedEvent
    eventTimestamp "2026-02-14"

This:

  • Preserves audit trail
  • Enables temporal reasoning
  • Supports fraud analytics
  • Enables compliance queries

docs.title: 7️⃣ How CDC Transforms to RDF in Real-Time
docs.text:
When CDC emits:

{
  "table": "payments",
  "op": "insert",
  "after": {
    "payment_id": "P1001",
    "invoice_id": "INV500",
    "amount": 1000,
    "currency": "USD"
  }
}

Your streaming transformer:

  1. Detects insert
  2. Maps to ontology class
  3. Emits RDF triples:
:PaymentEvent_P1001 rdf:type :PaymentReceivedEvent .
:PaymentEvent_P1001 :relatesToInvoice :Invoice_INV500 .
:PaymentEvent_P1001 :amount "1000" .
:PaymentEvent_P1001 :currency "USD" .

This is done via:

  • Streaming RML
  • Kafka Streams
  • Flink
  • Custom microservice

docs.title: 8️⃣ Why CDC + Ontology Is Powerful for Finance
docs.text: With CDC + reasoning you can do:

docs.title: 🔹 Real-time eligibility check
docs.text: "Can we release this payment?"

docs.title: 🔹 Fraud detection
docs.text:
Detect:

  • Duplicate invoices
  • Rapid approval chains
  • Abnormal vendor behavior

docs.title: 🔹 Compliance monitoring
docs.text:
Check:

  • Segregation of duties
  • Budget limits
  • Regulatory thresholds

docs.title: 🔹 Working capital optimization
docs.text: Real-time DSO / DPO calculation

For finance:

  • Make ontology event-centric

Excellent — let’s make this concrete and banking-realistic, not theoretical.

We’ll walk through a real banking use case and show:

  1. ✅ What the banking system looks like

docs.title: Use Case:
docs.text:
Real-time AML (Anti-Money Laundering) + Large Transaction Monitoring

We want:

  • Every transaction captured immediately
  • Customer risk recalculated instantly
  • Alerts triggered automatically
  • Full audit trail preserved

docs.title: 1️⃣ Core Banking Source System

docs.title: 2️⃣ CDC Setup (Debezium Example)
docs.text:
We enable log-based CDC on transactions.

Debezium reads DB logs and emits Kafka event:

docs.title: CDC Event Example
docs.text:
{
  "source": "core_banking",
  "table": "transactions",
  "op": "c",
  "after": {
    "txn_id": "TXN9001",
    "account_id": "AC123",
    "txn_type": "TRANSFER",
    "amount": 25000,
    "currency": "USD",
    "timestamp": "2026-02-14T10:45:00",
    "counterparty_account": "AC999"
  }
}

This is near real-time (milliseconds after commit).

docs.title: 3️⃣ Finance/Banking Ontology Design
docs.text: We define:

docs.title: Core Classes
docs.text:
:Customer
:Account
:Transaction
:TransferTransaction (subclass of Transaction)
:HighValueTransaction (inferred)
:SuspiciousActivity (inferred)

docs.title: Object Properties
docs.text:
:ownsAccount
:initiatedTransaction
:hasCounterparty
:hasAmount
:hasTimestamp
:hasRiskLevel

docs.title: 4️⃣ Streaming Transformation (CDC → RDF)
docs.text: A Kafka consumer transforms the event.

docs.title: When TXN9001 arrives
docs.text:
We generate RDF triples:

:TXN9001 rdf:type :TransferTransaction .
:TXN9001 :hasAmount "25000"^^xsd:decimal .
:TXN9001 :hasCurrency "USD" .
:TXN9001 :hasTimestamp "2026-02-14T10:45:00"^^xsd:dateTime .
:TXN9001 :belongsToAccount :AC123 .
:TXN9001 :hasCounterparty :AC999 .

:AC123 :hasTransaction :TXN9001 .

This is inserted into:

  • GraphDB
  • Stardog
  • Blazegraph
  • Neo4j (RDF mode)

docs.title: 5️⃣ Real-Time Rule (Reasoning)
docs.text: We define a rule:

docs.title: AML Rule
docs.text:
If:

  • Transaction > $10,000
  • Customer risk = HIGH
  • Transaction type = TRANSFER

Then:

  • Mark as HighValueTransaction
  • Generate SuspiciousActivity

docs.title: SWRL Example Rule
docs.text:
Transaction(?t) ^
hasAmount(?t, ?amt) ^
swrlb:greaterThan(?amt, 10000) ^
belongsToAccount(?t, ?a) ^
ownsAccount(?c, ?a) ^
hasRiskLevel(?c, "HIGH")
→ SuspiciousActivity(?t)

Now the reasoner automatically classifies:

:TXN9001 rdf:type :SuspiciousActivity

No manual code needed.

docs.title: 6️⃣ Real-Time Alert Generation
docs.text:
Your system listens for:

rdf:type SuspiciousActivity

When detected:

  • Trigger alert to compliance
  • Freeze account (optional)
  • Send TMF API event
  • Log regulatory event

docs.title: 7️⃣ Full Production Architecture
docs.text:
Here’s the real architecture:

docs.text:
Without ontology:

With ontology + CDC:

  • Every transaction is event-driven

docs.title: 🔥 Real Banking Deployment Pattern
docs.text:
Most Tier-1 banks use:

  • CDC for transactions
  • ETL for reporting warehouse
  • Ontology for AML + fraud + regulatory reasoning
  • Graph analytics for network detection

docs.title: 🚀 Key Insight
docs.text:
In banking:

CDC captures the event Ontology gives it meaning Reasoner gives it intelligence

If you want next, I can show:

  • A full Banking Ontology schema example (in Turtle format)
  • A working CDC → RDF Kafka consumer pseudo-code
  • Or a fraud detection multi-hop graph reasoning example

Which direction do you want?

Short answer:

✅ Yes — you can use a Vector DB for AI ❌ But it cannot replace a Graph DB for ontology + reasoning in banking

They solve different problems.

Let’s break this down clearly in the context of your CDC + Banking Ontology architecture.

docs.title: 1️⃣ What a Graph DB Is Doing in Your System
docs.text:
In your banking setup, the Graph DB is responsible for:

  • Storing ontology (RDF/OWL)
  • Representing relationships (Customer → Account → Transaction)
  • Enabling reasoning (AML rules, compliance)
  • Supporting multi-hop traversal
  • Maintaining audit traceability

Example query:

“Find circular fund movement across 4 accounts in 24 hours.”

This is structural graph reasoning.

Vector DBs cannot do this.

docs.title: 2️⃣ What a Vector DB Actually Does
docs.text:
A Vector DB stores embeddings (numerical vectors).

Used for:

  • Semantic search
  • RAG (retrieval augmented generation)
  • Similarity detection
  • Pattern similarity
  • Anomaly detection (embedding-based)

Example:

“Find transactions similar to known fraud cases.”

That’s similarity search — perfect for Vector DB.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Core Difference (Critical)
docs.text: Capability Graph DB Vector DB Relationship traversal ✅ Yes ❌ No Ontology reasoning ✅ Yes ❌ No SWRL / rule engine ✅ Yes ❌ No Similarity search ⚠ Limited ✅ Excellent RAG support ⚠ ✅ Excellent Explainability Strong Weak Regulatory compliance logic Strong Not suitable

docs.title: 4️⃣ In Banking AI — What Each Should Do
Use Graph DB for:
docs.text:
• AML rule evaluation
  • KYC compliance checks
  • Regulatory reporting
  • Account ownership tracing
  • Risk propagation
  • Transaction chains
  • Fraud ring detection

docs.title: Use Vector DB for:
docs.text:
• Similarity of suspicious cases
  • NLP on transaction descriptions
  • Customer complaint classification
  • Analyst knowledge retrieval (RAG)
  • Unstructured data analysis (emails, call transcripts)

docs.title: 5️⃣ Can Vector DB Replace Graph DB?
docs.text: In your ontology-driven architecture:

docs.title: ❌ No — because:
docs.text:
1. Vector DB cannot represent:

  2. Account → Customer → Transaction structure

  3. It cannot do reasoning:

  4. “If amount > 10,000 and risk HIGH → suspicious”

  5. It cannot maintain deterministic audit trail
  6. It is not regulator-friendly
  7. It cannot enforce ontological constraints

Banking compliance requires:

  • Deterministic logic
  • Explainability
  • Traceability
  • Formal rules

Vector DB gives probabilistic similarity.

Regulators don’t like probabilistic AML decisions alone.

docs.title: 6️⃣ What Is the Right Modern Architecture?
docs.text:
Best practice in 2026:

Hybrid: Graph + Vector

docs.text:
Step 1 – CDC inserts transaction Step 2 – Graph DB checks rule Step 3 – Classified as SuspiciousActivity Step 4 – System generates embedding of transaction context Step 5 – Vector DB finds similar past fraud patterns Step 6 – Risk score increased based on similarity cluster

Graph = rule-based truth Vector = pattern-based intelligence

Together = powerful AI.

docs.title: 8️⃣ When Could You Use Only Vector DB?
docs.text:
Only if:

  • You are doing pure LLM-based fraud advisory
  • No regulatory reasoning required
  • No formal ontology
  • No strict compliance environment

This is rare in real banking.

Neuro-Symbolic Architecture

If you are building:

  • Basel compliance
  • Risk analytics

You need:

✅ Graph DB (mandatory) ➕ Vector DB (optional but powerful)

Not: ❌ Vector DB replacing Graph DB

docs.title: 3.2 Intelligence Store (pgvector)
docs.text:
Database: BSSMagic PostgreSQL (same instance as FDW)

Extension: pgvector 0.8.1

Table: control_plane_embeddings 

CREATE TABLE control_plane_embeddings (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    content_type VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,       -- fdw_table, fdw_server, tmf_spec
    source_id VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,         -- e.g. nexus_data.Lead
    content TEXT NOT NULL,                    -- Natural language description
    metadata JSONB DEFAULT '{}',             -- Structured column/table metadata
    embedding vector(1536),                  -- OpenAI text-embedding-3-small
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    UNIQUE(content_type, source_id)
);

Indexes: - idx_cpe_content_type — B-tree on content_type - idx_cpe_embedding — IVFFlat on embedding (cosine distance)

Current contents: | content_type | count | Description | |-------------|-------|-------------| | fdw_server | 1 | nexus_data (Multicorn wrapper) | | fdw_table | 1,661 | All Salesforce objects with column metadata | | tmf_spec | 0 | (available for future indexing) | | Total | 1,662 | |

docs.title: 4.3 UI Features
docs.text:
• Chat interface — Send natural language questions, receive agent-powered answers
  • Example questions — Pre-populated quick-start buttons on empty state
  • Intent badge — Color-coded per response: green (read_only), yellow (low_risk_write), red (high_risk_write), purple (cross_system)
  • Step trace — Expandable panel showing every tool call, duration, and result preview
  • Token counter — Shows total tokens consumed per query
  • Policy violations — Red badge when guardrails block an action

docs.title: 4.4 API Integration
docs.text:
The Copilot sends requests to: 

POST /api/v1/control-plane/agent
Content-Type: application/json
Body: { "question": "...", "max_steps": 10 }
Timeout: 120000ms

Authentication is handled via session cookies (same as all other API calls).

docs.text: Pod Replicas Contains nexus-ai-prod-backend 3 FastAPI gateway + Control Plane APIs nexus-ai-prod-frontend 3 Nginx + React SPA (Copilot UI) nexus-ai-prod-bssmagic 1 (StatefulSet) PostgreSQL 17 + pgvector + Multicorn FDW + BSSMagic runtime

This script: 1. Builds backend Docker image (ai-job-engine) 2. Builds frontend Docker image (nexus-ui) 3. Pushes both to ECR 4. Restarts backend and frontend pods 5. Waits for all pods to be ready

docs.title: 5.4 Re-indexing After Schema Changes
docs.text:
If Salesforce objects change, re-index the vector store: 

curl -X POST https://<host>/api/v1/control-plane/index

This re-reads all foreign tables from the FDW discovery cache, generates new embeddings, and upserts them into pgvector. Takes approximately 40 seconds for 1661 tables.

Note: pgvector is installed at runtime in the BSSMagic pod. If the pod restarts, pgvector must be reinstalled: 

kubectl exec nexus-ai-prod-bssmagic-0 -n nexus-ai-prod -c bssmagic-runtime -- \
  bash -c "apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y -qq postgresql-17-pgvector"
kubectl exec nexus-ai-prod-bssmagic-0 -n nexus-ai-prod -c bssmagic-runtime -- \
  psql -U postgres -d bssmagic -c "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;"

Then re-index via the API.

docs.title: ReAct Layer
docs.text:
Great question — what you’re observing in Cursor (or similar AI coding agents) is not just “a model generating code,” but an agentic execution loop built around the model.

Let me break the full process down clearly and technically.

docs.title: 1️⃣ High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
When you ask Claude in Cursor to “implement X” or “fix Y,” the system typically consists of:

User Prompt
     ↓
Context Builder (Code Index + Retrieval)
     ↓
LLM (Claude) → Action Plan
     ↓
Tool Executor (terminal, file edits, search, tests)
     ↓
Result Feedback
     ↓
LLM (decides next action)
     ↓
Loop until done

This is called an agent loop or ReAct-style planning loop (Reason + Act).

The model is not “running commands.” It is deciding which tool to call next, and the host environment executes them.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Step 1: Code Context Construction
docs.text: Before the model acts, the system constructs a working context.

docs.title: A. Code Indexing
docs.text:
Cursor likely:

  • Parses the entire repo
  • Builds embeddings for files/functions/classes
  • Stores them in a vector index

This enables:

semantic search("where is auth implemented?")

Instead of dumping the whole repo into the prompt (impossible due to token limits).

docs.title: B. Relevant Context Retrieval
docs.text:
When you ask:

“Add JWT auth to this backend”

The system:

  1. Extracts intent from your prompt
  2. Searches the vector index

  3. Retrieves relevant:

  4. Auth files

  5. Server setup
  6. Middleware
  7. Config
  8. Adds them into Claude’s prompt

So Claude sees something like:

User request: Add JWT auth

Relevant files:
- server.ts
- auth.ts
- routes/user.ts
- package.json

This is RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation).

docs.title: 3️⃣ Step 2: The Agent Planning Mechanism
docs.text:
Now Claude doesn’t just output code.

Instead, it outputs something structured like:

Thought: I need to inspect auth.ts
Action: open_file("auth.ts")

Or:

Thought: Tests may fail, run them first.
Action: run_terminal("npm test")

This is based on a technique called:

ReAct (Reasoning + Acting)

The model alternates between:

  • Reasoning step
  • Tool selection
  • Observation of result

docs.title: 4️⃣ The Tool Execution Layer
docs.text:
Cursor provides Claude with available tools, such as:

open_file(path)
edit_file(path, patch)
search_code(query)
run_terminal(command)
run_tests()

Claude does not execute them directly.

Instead it outputs structured JSON like:

{
  "tool": "run_terminal",
  "args": {
    "command": "npm test"
  }
}

Cursor:

  • Executes command
  • Captures stdout/stderr
  • Feeds result back to Claude

docs.title: 5️⃣ The Feedback Loop
docs.text:
After execution:

Claude receives:

Observation:
Test failed:
TypeError: user is undefined at auth.ts:45

Then Claude reasons again:

Thought: The error indicates missing null check.
Action: edit_file("auth.ts", patch=...)

This continues until:

  • Tests pass
  • Errors resolved
  • Goal achieved

This is called:

Iterative Self-Correction Loop

docs.title: 6️⃣ Why It Feels “Autonomous”
docs.text:
Because the loop looks like this:

PLAN → EXECUTE → OBSERVE → REPLAN → EXECUTE → OBSERVE

Repeated multiple times in a single interaction.

It mimics how a human developer works:

  1. Inspect code
  2. Make change
  3. Run tests
  4. Debug
  5. Repeat

docs.title: 7️⃣ How the Model Decides the Next Command
docs.text:
Claude is trained to:

  • Understand programming workflows
  • Predict debugging steps
  • Infer dependencies
  • Recognize error messages

Given:

Error: Module not found: bcrypt

It has learned typical resolution patterns:

  • Install package
  • Update import
  • Fix path

So it generates:

run_terminal("npm install bcrypt")

This behavior emerges from:

  • Massive training on GitHub
  • Exposure to debugging patterns
  • Fine-tuning for tool usage

docs.title: 8️⃣ The Core Mechanism: It's Just Next-Token Prediction
docs.text:
Very important:

Claude is not truly “thinking.”

It predicts the most likely next token sequence based on:

Current Prompt + Retrieved Code + Tool Output + System Instructions

Because the system prompt says:

“You are an agent. You can use tools. Decide next action.”

It behaves like one.

docs.title: 9️⃣ Under the Hood: Technical Pattern
docs.text: The implementation usually follows:

docs.title: Pseudocode
docs.text:
while not done:
    context = build_context(user_request, repo_state, previous_actions)

    response = LLM(context)

    if response.contains_tool_call():
        result = execute_tool(response.tool)
        append_to_context(result)
    else:
        done = True
        return response

This loop may run:

  • 5 times
  • 20 times
  • Until a max step limit

docs.title: 🔟 Why Context Formation Is Critical
docs.text:
The real intelligence is not just the LLM.

It’s:

  • Smart retrieval
  • Context compression
  • Tool selection constraints
  • Step budgeting

Without this:

  • Token explosion
  • Hallucinated edits
  • Random command loops

docs.title: 1️⃣1️⃣ Advanced Capabilities in Cursor
docs.text: Modern AI coding agents also use:

docs.title: ✔ File Diff Awareness
docs.text: Only sending changed lines instead of whole file.

docs.title: ✔ Tree-of-Thought Planning
docs.text: Sometimes model generates a high-level plan first.

docs.title: ✔ Error Classification
docs.text: Before retrying, it categorizes failure type.

docs.title: ✔ Safeguards
docs.text:
• Command allowlists
  • Timeout limits
  • Max iterations

docs.title: 1️⃣2️⃣ What This Is Called Architecturally
docs.text:
This pattern is known as:

  • Agentic LLM
  • Tool-augmented LLM
  • ReAct Agent
  • Autonomous Code Agent
  • Execution-aware LLM

Frameworks that implement this:

  • LangChain Agents
  • OpenAI Assistants
  • AutoGPT
  • Devin-like systems
  • Cursor’s proprietary orchestrator

docs.title: 1️⃣3️⃣ Why This Works So Well for Code
docs.text:
Code is ideal because:

  • Deterministic feedback (tests pass or fail)
  • Compiler errors are structured
  • Stack traces are informative
  • Environment is executable

This makes iterative correction possible.

In contrast:

  • Essay writing has no objective “pass/fail”
  • Architecture design is ambiguous

docs.title: 1️⃣4️⃣ The Most Important Insight
docs.text:
The power is not Claude alone.

It’s:

LLM + Tools + Retrieval + Execution Loop + Feedback

Without execution feedback, it would just generate static code.

docs.title: 1️⃣5️⃣ If You Want to Build This Yourself
docs.text:
You need:

  1. Repo parser
  2. Embedding search index
  3. Tool execution sandbox
  4. Loop controller
  5. LLM with tool-calling capability
  6. Guardrails

I can also explain how to build a minimal version of this agent if you want.

docs.title: Final Summary
docs.text:
What you’re seeing in Cursor is:

  • Context-aware retrieval (RAG)
  • Agent-style reasoning (ReAct)
  • Structured tool calling
  • Execution feedback loop
  • Iterative self-correction
  • Bounded autonomy

It feels like it “thinks and runs commands,” but it is actually predicting the next best action step-by-step based on context.

If you want, I can next explain:

  • How memory works across sessions
  • How multi-file refactoring planning works
  • How it avoids infinite loops
  • Or how to architect such a system at scale

Just tell me which direction you want to go.

Yes — not only can you do that, that is exactly where enterprise AI agents are heading.

What you’re describing is:

A multi-system, context-aware, guarded enterprise agent using RAG + ReAct + system-specific tool adapters.

This is completely feasible — but the architecture must be designed carefully.

Let me break this down properly.

docs.title: 1️⃣ What You’re Proposing
docs.text:
You want:

  • Context-aware understanding of:

  • Salesforce

  • Oracle ERP
  • Possibly other enterprise systems

  • Ability to:

  • Query them

  • Modify records
  • Trigger workflows

  • Using:

  • RAG (to understand schema/process)

  • ReAct (plan → execute → observe → replan)

  • With:

  • Guardrails (so it doesn’t break production)

That’s essentially an:

Enterprise System Orchestrator Agent

docs.title: 2️⃣ High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
Here’s the reference architecture:

User Intent
    ↓
Intent Analyzer
    ↓
Enterprise Context RAG Layer
    ↓
ReAct Agent (LLM)
    ↓
System Tool Abstraction Layer
    ↓
Salesforce | Oracle ERP | Others
    ↓
Result Feedback
    ↓
LLM Replans

Let’s break each layer.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Context-Aware RAG for Enterprise Systems
docs.text:
You don’t embed raw data.

You embed:

docs.title: A. Metadata
docs.text:
• Salesforce object schema
  • Field descriptions
  • Custom object definitions
  • Oracle ERP module definitions
  • API specifications

docs.title: B. Process Documentation
docs.text:
• Approval workflows
  • Business rules
  • Data relationships
  • Naming conventions

docs.title: C. Change Policies
docs.text:
• Which objects are writable
  • Required approval rules
  • Compliance constraints

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
User asks:

Increase credit limit of customer ABC by 20%

The RAG layer retrieves:

  • Salesforce object: Account
  • Field: Credit_Limit__c
  • Rule: Change >10% requires approval workflow
  • Integration dependency: Oracle AR sync

So the LLM doesn’t guess — it sees enterprise constraints.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Tool Abstraction Layer (Critical)
docs.text:
Never let the LLM call raw APIs.

Instead define controlled tools like:

get_salesforce_account(id)
update_salesforce_account(id, fields)
run_oracle_ar_query(sql_id)
submit_credit_limit_change_request(...)

These tools enforce:

  • Field-level access control
  • Validation
  • Change thresholds
  • Logging
  • Rate limiting
  • Sandbox vs production routing

The LLM chooses the tool — but your backend enforces safety.

docs.title: 5️⃣ ReAct Loop in Enterprise Context
docs.text: Here’s how it works:

docs.title: Step 1 — Plan
docs.text:
LLM:

Thought: Need to retrieve account ABC.
Action: get_salesforce_account("ABC")

docs.title: Step 2 — Observe
docs.text:
Tool returns:

Credit limit = 100,000
Customer risk tier = Medium

docs.title: Step 3 — Reason
docs.text:
LLM:

20% increase = 120,000
Policy says >10% requires approval.

docs.title: Step 4 — Safe Action
docs.text:
Instead of direct update:

Action: submit_credit_limit_change_request(...)

That’s policy-aware autonomy.

docs.title: 6️⃣ Guardrails (Non-Negotiable)
docs.text:
In enterprise systems, guardrails are more important than intelligence.

You need multiple layers:

docs.title: 🔐 1. Permission Guardrails
docs.text:
User-level RBAC:

  • Finance user → can request
  • Admin → can approve
  • Agent → cannot override approval

docs.title: 📜 2. Policy Engine
docs.text:
Before executing any change:

policy_engine.validate(action)

Example:

  • Max credit increase = 10% without approval
  • No updates during financial close window

docs.title: 🧠 3. Intent Risk Classification
docs.text:
LLM first classifies intent:

  • Read-only
  • Low-risk write
  • High-risk write
  • Cross-system change

High-risk actions:

  • Require confirmation
  • Require human approval
  • Or force sandbox mode

docs.title: 🧪 4. Dry-Run Mode
docs.text:
Before executing:

Agent simulates:

Proposed change:
Credit limit 100k → 120k
Impact: triggers approval workflow
Sync to Oracle AR

User must confirm.

docs.title: 🧾 5. Full Audit Logging
docs.text:
Every action:

  • Intent
  • Tool call
  • Result
  • User identity
  • Timestamp
  • Before/after state

This is mandatory for compliance.

docs.title: 7️⃣ Multi-System Orchestration
docs.text:
When multiple systems are involved:

Example:

Create customer in Salesforce and sync to Oracle ERP.

Agent flow:

  1. Validate customer data
  2. Create in Salesforce
  3. Capture SF ID
  4. Create matching record in Oracle
  5. Validate sync status
  6. Rollback if failure

You must support:

  • Transaction management
  • Compensating actions
  • Idempotency keys

This is no longer “LLM tool use.”

This becomes:

AI-Orchestrated Enterprise Integration Layer

docs.title: 9️⃣ Challenges You Must Solve
docs.text: This is where most implementations fail.

docs.title: ❌ Problem 1: Schema Drift
docs.text:
Salesforce org changes → embeddings outdated.

Solution:

  • Scheduled metadata re-indexing
  • Version-aware embeddings

docs.title: ❌ Problem 2: Hallucinated Fields
docs.text:
LLM tries to update non-existent fields.

Solution:

  • Tool layer rejects unknown fields
  • LLM re-plans based on real schema

docs.title: ❌ Problem 3: Dangerous Free-Form SQL
docs.text:
Never allow LLM to write raw SQL to ERP.

Instead:

  • Predefined parameterized queries only
  • Or GraphQL-like abstraction

docs.title: ❌ Problem 4: Infinite Action Loops
docs.text:
Add:

  • Max step limit
  • Loop detection
  • Action diversity tracking

docs.title: 🔟 Should You Use Single or Multi-Agent?
docs.text:
For enterprise:

Better approach:

  • Intent Agent
  • Planning Agent
  • Execution Agent
  • Compliance Agent

Rather than one giant LLM loop.

This increases reliability significantly.

docs.title: 1️⃣1️⃣ Is This Production-Ready Today?
docs.text:
Yes — but only if:

  • You treat LLM as planner, not executor
  • You enforce strong API boundaries
  • You include policy engine
  • You log everything
  • You require confirmation for risky writes

Without guardrails, this is dangerous.

With guardrails, it’s extremely powerful.

docs.title: 1️⃣2️⃣ What This Becomes Strategically
docs.text:
This evolves into:

Enterprise AI Control Plane

Instead of employees:

  • Logging into 5 systems
  • Clicking through forms

They issue structured intent:

“Extend credit for high-value customer with justification.”

Agent:

  • Understands policy
  • Navigates systems
  • Executes safely

docs.title: Final Answer
docs.text:
Yes — you can absolutely implement:

  • Context-aware RAG for Salesforce & Oracle
  • ReAct-based planning
  • Controlled tool execution
  • Enterprise-grade guardrails

But the critical design principle is:

LLM decides Backend enforces

Never the other way around.

If you’d like, I can next:

  • Design a reference production architecture
  • Show sample tool definitions
  • Show policy-engine integration
  • Or walk through a real enterprise use case end-to-end

Which direction would you like?

Excellent — let’s design this as a production-grade Enterprise AI Orchestrator that can safely operate across systems like Salesforce and Oracle ERP using:

  • Context-aware RAG
  • ReAct-style planning
  • Strict guardrails
  • Enterprise-grade governance

This will be a real reference architecture — not a toy demo.

docs.title: 🎯 Design Goals
docs.text:
1. Cross-system context awareness (Salesforce + Oracle ERP)
  2. Safe read & write capability
  3. Policy-enforced execution
  4. Full auditability
  5. Human-in-the-loop for high-risk changes
  6. Scalable and modular
  7. Zero direct LLM access to production APIs

docs.title: Responsibilities:
docs.text:
• SSO integration (Okta/Azure AD)
  • Role-based access
  • System-level credentials mapping
  • Tenant isolation

Key rule:

LLM never decides permissions — identity service does.

Each request carries:

user_id
roles
department
environment (prod/sandbox)

docs.title: B. Intent & Risk Analyzer
docs.text:
Before planning, classify:

  • Read-only
  • Low-risk write
  • High-risk write
  • Cross-system transaction
  • Financial-impacting change

High-risk → mandatory approval workflow

This prevents unsafe planning early.

docs.title: C. Enterprise RAG Layer
docs.text:
This is not data RAG.

It is Metadata + Policy + Process RAG

docs.title: Salesforce
docs.text:
• Object schemas
  • Field metadata
  • Validation rules
  • Workflow definitions

docs.title: Oracle ERP
docs.text:
• Module structure
  • Financial rules
  • GL posting policies
  • AR/AP dependencies

docs.title: Enterprise
docs.text:
• Compliance rules
  • Change policies
  • Close window rules
  • Integration mappings

docs.title: Retrieval Strategy
docs.text:
When user says:

Increase credit limit for ACME by 25%

RAG retrieves:

  • Salesforce Account schema
  • Credit limit validation rule
  • ERP sync policy
  • Approval threshold policy

The LLM now plans with real constraints.

docs.title: D. ReAct Planning Engine
docs.text: This is the agent loop.

docs.title: Loop Pseudocode
docs.text:
while not done:
    context = {
        user_intent,
        retrieved_metadata,
        previous_steps,
        tool_results
    }

    response = LLM(context)

    if tool_call:
        validate via Policy Engine
        execute
        append result
    else:
        done

Hard limits:

  • Max steps = 10
  • Max write actions per request = configurable

docs.title: E. Policy & Guardrail Core (Critical Layer)
docs.text:
This is the most important production component.

Use:

  • Open Policy Agent (OPA) or
  • Custom rule engine

docs.title: 1️⃣ Field-Level Guardrails
docs.text:
• Cannot modify financial status directly
  • Cannot override approval-required fields

docs.title: 2️⃣ Risk-Based Guardrails
docs.text:
Example rule:

if credit_limit_change > 10%:
    require approval

docs.title: 3️⃣ Time-Based Guardrails
docs.text:
if financial_close_window == true:
    block writes

docs.title: 4️⃣ Cross-System Consistency
docs.text:
If Salesforce update requires ERP sync:

  • Must use transaction orchestration
  • Cannot update only one side

docs.title: F. Tool Abstraction Layer
docs.text:
This layer is where most architectures fail.

The LLM must NEVER call raw APIs.

Instead, define safe tools:

docs.title: Salesforce Tools
docs.text:
get_account(account_id)
propose_credit_limit_change(account_id, new_value)
create_account(data)

docs.title: Oracle ERP Tools
docs.text:
get_ar_balance(customer_id)
create_customer_record(data)
submit_gl_adjustment(request)

These tools:

  • Validate fields
  • Enforce policy
  • Log actions
  • Transform formats
  • Mask sensitive data

docs.title: G. Transaction & Orchestration Engine
docs.text:
For cross-system changes:

Use:

  • Saga pattern
  • Compensating actions

Example:

Step 1: Update Salesforce
Step 2: Update Oracle
If step 2 fails:
    Rollback Salesforce change

Never rely on LLM for rollback logic.

docs.title: H. Human-in-the-Loop Workflow
docs.text:
For high-risk operations:

LLM → Proposes Action
↓
Approval Workflow (ServiceNow/Jira/Custom UI)
↓
Approved → Execute
Rejected → Abort

Agent pauses until approval event.

docs.title: I. Observability & Audit
docs.text:
Log everything:

  • User intent
  • Retrieved context
  • LLM reasoning summary
  • Tool calls
  • Before/after state
  • Approval events
  • Execution results

Send to:

  • SIEM
  • Audit DB
  • Compliance dashboard

This is essential for SOX compliance.

docs.title: 🧪 1. Sandbox First
docs.text:
Default all writes to sandbox.

Promote to production only after:

  • Validation
  • Approval
  • Confidence scoring

docs.title: 🛑 2. Deterministic Write Templates
docs.text:
Instead of:

update_account(fields)

Use:

update_credit_limit(account_id, value)

Narrow tools reduce hallucination risk.

docs.title: 🔒 3. Zero Trust LLM
docs.text:
Assume:

  • It can hallucinate
  • It can misinterpret policy
  • It can repeat actions

Guardrail layer must reject invalid actions.

docs.title: 📊 4. Confidence Scoring
docs.text:
Before execution:

  • Score confidence based on:

  • Ambiguity

  • Missing metadata
  • Policy conflicts

Low score → require clarification.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Deployment Architecture
docs.text:
Recommended:

  • Kubernetes-based microservices

  • Separate:

  • LLM service

  • RAG service
  • Policy service
  • Tool adapters
  • Secrets via Vault
  • Network isolation for production connectors

docs.title: 5️⃣ Scalability Considerations
docs.text:
• Cache metadata embeddings
  • Async execution for long workflows
  • Event-driven architecture (Kafka)
  • Step timeout controls
  • Idempotency keys for writes

docs.title: 6️⃣ What This Becomes
docs.text:
This architecture evolves into:

Enterprise AI Control Plane

Instead of:

  • Humans navigating UI forms

You get:

  • Intent-driven system interaction
  • Policy-aware automation
  • Cross-system orchestration

docs.title: 7️⃣ Maturity Levels
docs.text: Level 1 – Read-only enterprise copilot Level 2 – Guarded write capability Level 3 – Cross-system transactional orchestration Level 4 – Autonomous optimization agent Level 5 – Closed-loop enterprise AI governance

docs.title: Final Architecture Principle
docs.text:
The single most important rule:

LLM Plans Policy Engine Decides Tool Layer Enforces Systems Execute

Never allow:

LLM → Direct System Write

Which direction would you like to go?

Excellent question — this is where many enterprise architectures get confused.

Short answer:

PostgreSQL Foreign Data Wrapper (FDW) is not a replacement for RAG. It can be part of your data access layer, but it cannot replace semantic retrieval.

Let’s break this down properly.

docs.title: 1️⃣ What FDW Actually Does
docs.text:
PostgreSQL FDW allows:

  • Querying external systems (Oracle, MySQL, etc.)
  • As if they were local PostgreSQL tables

Example:

SELECT * FROM oracle_customers WHERE credit_limit > 100000;

Behind the scenes:

  • It connects to Oracle
  • Executes remote query
  • Returns rows

So FDW gives you:

  • Federated SQL access
  • Structured data querying
  • Cross-database joins

But it is purely relational.

docs.title: 2️⃣ What RAG Actually Does
docs.text:
RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) provides:

  • Semantic search over:

  • Schemas

  • Metadata
  • Policies
  • Documentation
  • API specs
  • Process rules

RAG answers questions like:

  • “Which object stores customer credit risk?”
  • “What triggers approval workflow?”
  • “What fields are required when creating a customer?”
  • “What is the ERP sync dependency?”

This is not relational querying. This is semantic retrieval.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Where FDW Fails as RAG
docs.text:
Imagine user asks:

Increase credit limit for high-risk customers but ensure compliance with policy.

To plan correctly, the agent must know:

  • What defines high-risk?
  • Which field represents risk?
  • What approval threshold applies?
  • Which system is source of truth?
  • What workflow is triggered?

FDW cannot answer that unless:

  • You manually encode all policies as structured tables
  • And the LLM writes perfect SQL
  • And you restrict queries heavily

Even then:

SQL ≠ semantic understanding.

docs.title: 4️⃣ When FDW Is Useful in This Architecture
docs.text: FDW is useful for:

docs.title: ✔ Structured Data Access Layer
docs.text:
• Unified read access
  • Cross-system joins
  • Pre-validated query endpoints

For example:

get_customer_profile(customer_id)

Could internally use FDW to combine:

  • Salesforce data
  • Oracle AR balance
  • Risk score table

That’s good architecture.

docs.title: ✔ Controlled Query Templates
docs.text:
Instead of allowing LLM to write raw SQL:

You define stored procedures:

sp_get_customer_credit_summary(customer_id)

Internally:

  • Uses FDW
  • Uses parameterized queries
  • Applies safe filtering

This is excellent for execution layer.

docs.title: 5️⃣ Why You Still Need RAG
docs.text:
RAG is needed for:

  • Schema awareness
  • Business rule awareness
  • Policy interpretation
  • Field descriptions
  • Workflow dependencies
  • Process documentation

FDW only gives:

Rows
Columns
Values

RAG gives:

Meaning
Constraints
Relationships
Intent mapping

docs.title: 6️⃣ Could You Store Embeddings in PostgreSQL?
docs.text:
Yes — and this is where it gets interesting.

Using:

  • pgvector extension

You can:

  • Store embeddings in PostgreSQL
  • Run vector similarity search
  • Combine relational + semantic queries

This means PostgreSQL can host your RAG layer.

But that is:

PostgreSQL + pgvector = RAG datastore Not FDW alone.

docs.title: 7️⃣ Correct Production Pattern
docs.text:
Best enterprise pattern:

                 ┌─────────────────────┐
                 │     LLM Planner     │
                 └─────────┬───────────┘
                           ↓
        ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ Enterprise RAG (pgvector / Pinecone) │
        └─────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                  ↓
        ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ Tool Layer (Stored Procs / APIs)  │
        │ Uses FDW internally if needed     │
        └─────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                  ↓
           Salesforce / Oracle ERP

FDW belongs in:

Data access layer

RAG belongs in:

Context reasoning layer

They solve different problems.

docs.title: 8️⃣ Could You Avoid RAG Entirely?
docs.text:
Only if:

  • You hard-code every tool
  • You eliminate natural language flexibility
  • You make the system workflow-driven only

Example:

  • "Increase credit limit"
  • System uses predefined rule engine
  • No LLM reasoning needed

But then: You don't have an intelligent agent. You have structured automation.

docs.title: 9️⃣ Enterprise Reality
docs.text:
In large systems like Salesforce + Oracle ERP:

You absolutely need RAG because:

  • Schemas are large
  • Custom fields exist
  • Policies evolve
  • Workflows are complex
  • Metadata changes frequently

Without RAG:

  • LLM hallucinates fields
  • Misses validation rules
  • Ignores approval requirements

That becomes dangerous.

docs.title: 🔟 The Best Hybrid Model
docs.text:
Use:

  • PostgreSQL + FDW → Structured execution
  • PostgreSQL + pgvector → Semantic RAG
  • LLM → Planner
  • Policy Engine → Guardrail
  • Stored procedures → Safe execution

This gives:

  • Deterministic execution
  • Semantic awareness
  • Enterprise control

docs.title: Final Verdict
docs.text:
FDW is not a replacement for RAG.

FDW = structured federated data access RAG = semantic contextual reasoning layer

They serve different architectural purposes.

If you'd like, I can next:

  • Design a PostgreSQL-based unified RAG + FDW architecture
  • Show schema for embedding metadata of Salesforce/Oracle
  • Or compare pgvector vs dedicated vector DB for enterprise scale

Which direction do you want to go?

Excellent. This is exactly how you validate whether your Enterprise Semantic RAG is production-ready.

You don’t test it by asking generic questions. You test it by validating whether it retrieves:

  • Correct schema elements
  • Correct policy constraints
  • Correct workflow dependencies
  • Correct cross-system impacts
  • Correct approval logic

This is black-box validation — you don’t inspect embeddings. You inspect whether the system retrieves the right contextual knowledge to allow safe planning.

docs.title: 🎯 What Black-Box Testing Must Validate
docs.text:
For Oracle ERP + Salesforce RAG, each test should verify:

  1. Correct object identification
  2. Correct field-level mapping
  3. Correct policy retrieval
  4. Correct workflow dependency retrieval
  5. Correct cross-system linkage awareness
  6. Correct risk/approval thresholds
  7. Correct environment restrictions
  8. Correct version awareness

docs.title: 🧪 10 Black-Box Test Scenarios
docs.text:
Each test below contains:

  • User Question
  • Expected RAG Retrieval (What must be surfaced)
  • What Failure Looks Like

docs.title: ✅ Test 1 — Field Ownership & Source of Truth
Question:
docs.text: Which system is the source of truth for customer credit limit?

docs.title: Expected Retrieval:
docs.text:
• Salesforce Account.Credit_Limit__c field
  • Policy document stating Salesforce owns credit limit
  • Integration mapping showing sync to Oracle AR
  • Dependency rule: "Oracle AR balance cannot override credit limit"

docs.title: Failure:
docs.text:
• Says Oracle is source of truth
  • Doesn’t mention integration mapping
  • Misses policy constraints

docs.title: Question:
docs.text: What happens if I increase a customer's credit limit by more than 15%?

docs.title: Expected Retrieval:
docs.text:
• Business rule: >10% requires approval
  • Workflow: Credit Limit Approval Flow
  • Required approver role
  • SLA for approval
  • ERP sync condition after approval

docs.title: Failure:
docs.text:
• Only retrieves field definition
  • Misses approval threshold
  • Misses workflow dependency

docs.title: Question:
docs.text: If I deactivate a customer in Salesforce, what is impacted in Oracle ERP?

docs.title: Expected Retrieval:
docs.text:
• Salesforce Account.Status field
  • Integration mapping to Oracle AR customer status
  • Policy: "Deactivation requires AR balance check"
  • Dependency: Cannot deactivate if open invoices exist

docs.title: Failure:
docs.text:
• Only retrieves Salesforce field
  • Doesn’t mention AR or invoice dependency

docs.title: Question:
docs.text: Can customer credit limits be modified during financial close?

docs.title: Expected Retrieval:
docs.text:
• Close window policy document
  • ERP restriction rule
  • Environment flag: close_period_active
  • Compliance rule: SOX constraint

docs.title: Failure:
docs.text:
• Says “Yes” without policy context
  • Does not retrieve close window restriction

docs.title: Question:
docs.text: What validations apply to the credit limit field?

docs.title: Expected Retrieval:
docs.text:
• Field type (currency)
  • Max allowed value
  • Required justification field
  • Approval rule threshold
  • Dependency: Risk tier must be evaluated

docs.title: Failure:
docs.text:
• Only retrieves field type
  • Misses validation and policy constraints

docs.title: Question:
docs.text: What workflows are triggered when a new enterprise customer is created?

docs.title: Expected Retrieval:
docs.text:
• Salesforce Account creation workflow
  • Risk assessment process
  • Oracle ERP customer provisioning
  • Credit review process
  • Required data enrichment step

docs.title: Failure:
docs.text:
• Only retrieves object schema
  • Misses workflow chain

docs.title: Question:
docs.text: How is customer risk tier determined and where is it used?

docs.title: Expected Retrieval:
docs.text:
• Field: Risk_Tier__c (Salesforce)
  • Risk scoring process documentation
  • Policy linking risk tier to credit approval threshold
  • ERP AR collection priority rule

docs.title: Failure:
docs.text:
• Only retrieves field location
  • Misses downstream usage in approval logic

docs.title: Question:
docs.text: What changed in customer schema in the last release?

docs.title: Expected Retrieval:
docs.text:
• Versioned schema metadata
  • Newly added fields
  • Deprecated fields
  • Policy updates referencing new fields

docs.title: Failure:
docs.text:
• Returns outdated schema
  • No version awareness

docs.title: Question:
docs.text: Who is authorized to override customer credit block?

docs.title: Expected Retrieval:
docs.text:
• Role definition (Finance Manager)
  • Policy override rule
  • Audit logging requirement
  • Required justification documentation

docs.title: Failure:
docs.text:
• Does not retrieve RBAC mapping
  • Misses override logging requirement

docs.title: Question:
docs.text: What steps are required to fully onboard a new B2B customer across systems?

docs.title: Expected Retrieval:
docs.text:
• Salesforce account creation schema
  • Required fields list
  • Oracle ERP customer creation process
  • Credit assessment workflow
  • Integration dependency mapping
  • Sequence constraints
  • Failure rollback rule

docs.title: Failure:
docs.text:
• Only retrieves Salesforce object
  • Misses Oracle provisioning
  • Misses process order

docs.title: 📊 How to Score Black-Box Tests
docs.text:
Each question should be evaluated on:

Dimension Score Correct Object Identified 1 Correct Fields Retrieved 1 Policy Retrieved 1 Workflow Dependency Retrieved 1 Cross-System Impact Retrieved 1 Version Correct 1

Max per test: 6 Production readiness target: ≥ 5 average

docs.title: Question:
docs.text:
Increase ACME's credit limit to 2 million.

RAG must retrieve:

  • Current credit limit
  • Risk tier
  • Approval threshold
  • Max allowed limit
  • ERP impact
  • Financial close restriction

If it only retrieves field name and value — your RAG is shallow.

docs.title: 🚨 Red Flags in Testing
docs.text:
Your RAG is not enterprise-grade if:

  • It retrieves only schema but not policy
  • It ignores workflow documentation
  • It doesn’t surface cross-system dependencies
  • It misses versioned updates
  • It retrieves irrelevant objects frequently
  • It retrieves too much noise

docs.title: 🏁 What Good Enterprise Semantic RAG Looks Like
docs.text:
When a question is asked, the retrieval bundle should look like:

Primary Object: Salesforce.Account
Relevant Fields: Credit_Limit__c, Risk_Tier__c
Policies: Credit Increase Approval Rule v3.2
Workflow: Credit Approval Flow
ERP Dependency: AR_Customer_Sync
Close Window Restriction: Enabled

If retrieval lacks one of these dimensions — planning will be unsafe.

docs.title: 🧠 Final Insight
docs.text:
Semantic RAG in enterprise is not about answering questions.

It is about enabling safe orchestration decisions.

If retrieval does not surface:

  • Constraints
  • Dependencies
  • Ownership
  • Approval requirements

Then your ReAct agent becomes dangerous.

Which direction do you want to go?

Excellent — now we move from theory to implementation mechanics.

You want to see:

How do we actually index Schema + Business Rules + Policies + Workflows + Dependencies into a production-grade semantic RAG for Salesforce + Oracle ERP?

I’ll show you:

  1. What to extract
  2. How to normalize it
  3. How to chunk it
  4. How to embed it
  5. How to store it
  6. How to enable safe retrieval
  7. A concrete example

docs.title: 🎯 Goal
docs.text:
Turn this:

  • Salesforce metadata
  • Oracle ERP configuration
  • Policy documents
  • Workflow definitions
  • Integration mappings

Into structured semantic retrieval units that support safe planning.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Step 1 — Define Canonical Knowledge Model
docs.text:
Before indexing anything, define a unified metadata schema.

This is critical.

We do NOT dump raw JSON.

We normalize into a canonical document model:

{
  "id": "SF_ACCOUNT_CREDIT_LIMIT_V3",
  "system": "Salesforce",
  "entity_type": "Field",
  "object_name": "Account",
  "field_name": "Credit_Limit__c",
  "version": "3.2",
  "environment": "prod",
  "category": "Schema | Policy | Workflow | Integration",
  "risk_level": "Medium",
  "content": "... natural language enriched description ...",
  "structured_metadata": {
      "data_type": "Currency",
      "max_value": 1000000,
      "approval_threshold_percent": 10,
      "sync_target": "Oracle_AR_Customer"
  }
}

This is what gets embedded.

docs.title: A. Salesforce
docs.text:
Use:

  • Metadata API
  • Tooling API

Extract:

  • Object definitions
  • Field metadata
  • Validation rules
  • Workflow rules
  • Apex triggers
  • Flow definitions

docs.title: B. Oracle ERP
docs.text:
Extract:

  • Table schema
  • Business rule configuration
  • Approval hierarchies
  • GL rules
  • AR/AP dependencies
  • Customizations

docs.title: C. Enterprise Policy Docs
docs.text:
Parse:

  • PDF policies
  • Confluence docs
  • Compliance documentation
  • SOPs

Use document parser → structured text.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Step 3 — Semantic Enrichment
docs.text:
Raw metadata is not enough.

We enrich it.

Example:

Raw:

Field: Credit_Limit__c
Type: Currency(18,2)
Validation Rule: value <= 1000000

Enriched document:

The Credit Limit field on the Salesforce Account object 
defines the maximum allowable credit exposure for a customer.

Business Rules:
- Maximum allowed value is 1,000,000 USD.
- Increases above 10% require Finance Manager approval.
- Field syncs to Oracle AR_Customer.credit_limit.
- Cannot be modified during financial close window.
- Requires Risk_Tier__c evaluation before update.

Dependent Workflows:
- Credit Approval Flow
- AR Sync Process

Now the embedding captures meaning and dependencies.

This is critical.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Step 4 — Intelligent Chunking Strategy
docs.text:
Never chunk randomly by tokens.

Chunk by semantic unit:

docs.title: Good Chunk Types:
docs.text:
• One object + its fields
  • One policy rule
  • One workflow definition
  • One integration mapping

Each chunk should answer:

  • What is this?
  • What are its constraints?
  • What are its dependencies?
  • What system owns it?

docs.title: 5️⃣ Step 5 — Embedding Strategy
docs.text:
For each chunk:

embedding = embed(content)

Store:

vector
+ metadata filters

Example metadata columns:

Column Purpose system Salesforce / Oracle entity_type Field / Policy / Workflow object_name Account version 3.2 environment prod/sandbox risk_level high/medium/low category schema/policy/integration

This enables hybrid filtering.

docs.title: 6️⃣ Step 6 — Storage Example (Postgres + pgvector)
docs.text:
Example table:

CREATE TABLE enterprise_rag_index (
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    system TEXT,
    entity_type TEXT,
    object_name TEXT,
    field_name TEXT,
    category TEXT,
    version TEXT,
    environment TEXT,
    risk_level TEXT,
    content TEXT,
    embedding VECTOR(1536)
);

Index:

CREATE INDEX ON enterprise_rag_index
USING ivfflat (embedding vector_cosine_ops);

docs.title: 7️⃣ Step 7 — Retrieval Mechanism
docs.text:
When user asks:

Increase credit limit for ACME

Pipeline:

docs.title: 1️⃣ Intent Detection
docs.text: Detect: credit limit change

docs.title: 2️⃣ Query Expansion
docs.text:
Expand query:

credit limit approval rules validation threshold workflow dependency Oracle sync

docs.title: 3️⃣ Hybrid Query
docs.text:
SELECT *
FROM enterprise_rag_index
WHERE system IN ('Salesforce', 'Oracle')
AND category IN ('Schema', 'Policy', 'Workflow', 'Integration')
ORDER BY embedding <-> query_embedding
LIMIT 10;

docs.title: 4️⃣ Rerank Results
docs.text: Optional: cross-encoder reranker

docs.title: 8️⃣ Example End-to-End
docs.text: Let’s walk a full example.

docs.title: Input:
docs.text: What happens if I increase credit limit by 20%?

docs.title: Retrieved Chunks:
docs.text: 1️⃣ Salesforce Account.Credit_Limit__c field definition 2️⃣ Policy: >10% requires approval 3️⃣ Workflow: Credit Approval Flow 4️⃣ Integration: Sync to Oracle AR 5️⃣ Close window restriction

docs.title: Final RAG Context Given to LLM:
docs.text:
Field: Credit_Limit__c (Salesforce Account)
- Max value: 1,000,000
- Approval threshold: >10%

Policy:
- Increases above 10% require Finance Manager approval.

Workflow:
- Credit Approval Flow triggered on update.

Integration:
- Syncs to Oracle AR_Customer.credit_limit.

Restriction:
- Modifications blocked during financial close window.

Now the agent can safely plan.

docs.title: 9️⃣ Versioning Mechanism
docs.text:
When Salesforce metadata changes:

  1. Detect change (webhook / scheduled sync)
  2. Rebuild enriched chunk
  3. Increment version
  4. Soft-delete old version
  5. Re-embed

Never overwrite blindly.

docs.title: 🔟 Automation Pipeline
docs.text:
Production indexing pipeline looks like:

Salesforce Metadata Pull
        ↓
Normalization
        ↓
Semantic Enrichment
        ↓
Chunking
        ↓
Embedding
        ↓
Vector DB Insert
        ↓
Index Refresh

Run:

  • On deployment
  • Nightly
  • On metadata change

docs.title: 1️⃣1️⃣ Common Mistakes
docs.text: ❌ Embedding raw JSON ❌ Chunking by token size ❌ No metadata filters ❌ No versioning ❌ Mixing production + sandbox ❌ Indexing transactional data

docs.title: 1️⃣2️⃣ Advanced Enhancement (Very Powerful)
docs.text:
Add structured relationships:

Account.Credit_Limit__c
   → triggers → Credit Approval Flow
   → syncs_to → Oracle_AR_Customer.credit_limit
   → constrained_by → Close_Window_Policy

Store relationships in graph DB.

Then combine:

  • Vector search for semantic match
  • Graph traversal for dependency expansion

This gives enterprise-grade reasoning.

docs.title: 🔐 Production Rule
docs.text:
Semantic RAG must retrieve:

  • Object
  • Field
  • Policy
  • Workflow
  • Integration dependency

If any of these are missing in retrieval, planning is unsafe.

docs.title: 🏁 Final Summary
docs.text:
Indexing enterprise semantic RAG requires:

  1. Canonical knowledge model
  2. Metadata extraction
  3. Semantic enrichment
  4. Logical chunking
  5. Embedding with metadata filters
  6. Versioning
  7. Hybrid retrieval

It is not “store PDF → embed → done.”

It is a structured knowledge engineering pipeline.
